I’ve been farming these fields in Quzhou for over forty years. I only finished middle school, but the land is what I know best. At sixty-four, I don’t have the strength or the desire to chase risky cash crops that need constant hand labor like cotton or stevia. My back aches after a day of bending, and my children are working in the city, so it’s mostly me and my wife now. The safest, most reliable system here on the North China Plain is still the wheat–maize double crop. The machinery for sowing and harvesting is easy to hire, the grain traders come right to the village, and the government gives a minimum purchase price for wheat, which lets me sleep at night. 

This year I will keep five mu in the winter wheat–summer maize rotation. I know this soil, and I know that if I plough before wheat and leave the stubble for the maize, the yields hold steady. I’ll also plant one mu of spring peanuts. Peanuts don’t need as much irrigation as maize, they fix a bit of nitrogen, and my family likes having our own cooking oil. More importantly, they break the monoculture and keep the soil from getting too tired. For the wheat I’ll use an improved variety like Shimai or Liangxing—seeds I’ve saved or bought from the local cooperative—and for the maize I’ll buy hybrid seed packages such as Nongda 372 because the hybrids outyield anything else in our short summer window. I’ll fertilize based on what the extension agent recommended years ago: a basal compound fertilizer and topdressing with urea. I’ll irrigate the wheat four times—overwintering, jointing, heading, and filling—because groundwater is still accessible from our well, and the maize twice if the rains are normal. I keep pesticide use to the minimum needed: a herbicide at sowing and one or two sprays for insects and fungi, no more. I’m too old to waste money on chemicals the crops don’t need.
